question: An 11-year-old girl is admitted with progressive abdominal distension over 3 weeks and a history of jaundice. During abdominal examination, you find dullness in the flanks that shifts with position change. Which ONE clinical sign has BEST been demonstrated?

answers.text: Organomegaly — shifting dullness is the percussion sign of an enlarged liver or spleen.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Shifting dullness is NOT the sign for organomegaly. Organomegaly is detected by percussion (dullness over the organ) and palpation (ballottement for kidney, bimanual for liver edge). Shifting dullness specifically tests for FREE FLUID (ascites) in the abdomen.

answers.text: Ascites — shifting dullness (dullness in the flanks that shifts to the upper side when the patient turns) indicates free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Shifting dullness is the standard clinical sign for ascites. When the patient lies supine, fluid settles in the flanks (dull on percussion). When turned to one side, the fluid shifts away from the uppermost flank (which becomes resonant). ≥500 mL of free fluid is required for shifting dullness to be detectable. The fluid thrill (palpated wave in a very large ascites) and puddle sign (for <100 mL) are complementary. In portal hypertension, ascites = transudate (SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL).

answers.text: Splenomegaly — shifting dullness in the flanks with position change is the percussion method for an enlarged spleen.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Splenomegaly is assessed by percussion (Traube's space — left lower chest resonance lost when spleen enlarges) and palpation (starting at right iliac fossa, moving toward left hypochondrium). Shifting dullness tests for free fluid, not spleen size.

answers.text: Peritonitis — shifting dullness is the hallmark sign of peritoneal inflammation and indicates a surgical emergency.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Peritonitis presents with guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness — NOT shifting dullness. Shifting dullness indicates free fluid (ascites or haemoperitoneum), not inflammation of the peritoneum per se.

overallFeedback.feedback: Shifting dullness = free peritoneal fluid (ascites). In a jaundiced child with abdominal distension, this strongly suggests liver disease with portal hypertension or hypoalbuminaemia. Organomegaly is assessed separately by palpation + percussion of the liver and spleen.

Correct. Shifting dullness = ascites (free fluid ≥500 mL). In a child with jaundice and abdominal distension, ascites indicates portal hypertension or hypoalbuminaemia from liver disease. The SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient) ≥1.1 g/dL distinguishes portal hypertension (transudate) from low-albumin/malignant ascites.
